text:
The line graph illustrates how many commuters in a European city used cars, buses and bicycles to travel to work at five-year intervals between 2000 and 2020. Figures are given in thousands.

Overall, car use declined over the period, whereas bus use rose steadily, so that buses overtook cars as the most popular mode of commuting by the end. Cycling remained marginal and virtually unchanged throughout.

Cars were the dominant choice at the start of the period, with 420 thousand commuters in 2000. This figure climbed to a peak of 450 thousand in 2005 before dropping to 430 thousand in 2010. The decline then accelerated, with the number falling to 380 thousand in 2015 and to 300 thousand in 2020, a decrease of 120 thousand compared with the starting point.

Bus use followed the opposite course. Starting at 210 thousand, it grew consistently in every period, reaching 260 thousand in 2010 and 330 thousand in 2020, an increase of 120 thousand. The two lines crossed between 2015, when buses stood at 300 thousand and cars at 380 thousand, and 2020. Cycling, by contrast, fluctuated only between 40 and 42 thousand.

issues.quote: both stood at 300 thousand for buses and 380 thousand for cars
issues.correction: the figures stood at 300 thousand for buses and 380 thousand for cars
issues.reason: 'Both' is incorrect here because the two modes had different figures in 2015, so the sentence should refer to the two figures rather than saying both stood at those values.

text:
The line graph compares the proportion of households with internet access in three countries between 2004 and 2022, with figures expressed as percentages.

Overall, internet access increased markedly in all three nations throughout the period. Country A remained the leader from start to finish, while Country C consistently recorded the lowest levels. Although the gap between A and B narrowed substantially by 2022, Country C still lagged behind the other two despite considerable growth.

In 2004, Country A already had internet access in 32% of households, far ahead of Country B at 12% and Country C at just 5%. By 2007, the figures had risen to 51%, 20%, and 8% respectively, and this upward pattern continued in 2010, when Country A reached 68%. In the same year, Country B reached 35%, exactly 21 percentage points above Country C, which stood at 14%.

After 2010, growth slowed in Country A but remained strong in the other two countries. Country A increased from 80% in 2013 to 88% in 2016, before edging up to 93% in 2019 and 95% in 2022. Country B followed a steeper trajectory, rising from 55% in 2013 to 70% in 2016, then to 82% and finally 90%. Country C also accelerated, moving from 25% to 41%, 58%, and 72% across the same years.

issues.quote: Over the same year, Country B climbed to 35%
issues.correction: In the same year, Country B stood at 35%
issues.reason: "Over the same year" is unidiomatic, and "climbed" is inappropriate for a single year's figure.

issues.quote: exactly 21 percentage points above Country C, which stood at 14%
issues.correction: exactly 21 percentage points above Country C, which stood at 14%
issues.reason: 35 minus 14 is 21, so this is correct; no change needed.

issues.quote: Growth became especially pronounced after 2010.
issues.correction: Growth in Country B and Country C became especially pronounced after 2010.
issues.reason: Country A's growth slowed after 2010, so the general statement does not match the data.

text:
The line graph compares how many domestic and overseas tourists came to a coastal town in each month of 2023, with figures given in thousands.

Overall, both categories followed a clear seasonal pattern, climbing from a winter low to a pronounced peak in August before declining toward the end of the year. Domestic visitors outnumbered overseas visitors in every month, and the gap was widest at the height of summer.

Domestic arrivals began the year at 12 thousand in January and dipped to their lowest level, 11 thousand, in February. They then grew steadily to 30 thousand in May, before surging to 45 thousand in June and 68 thousand in July. The peak came in August, at 72 thousand, after which the figure fell sharply to 40 thousand in September and 25 thousand in October.

Overseas visitors showed a similar but much smaller pattern. Numbers stood at just 3 thousand in January and February, rose to 14 thousand in May and reached a high of 28 thousand in August. They then dropped to 18 thousand in September and 9 thousand in October. After a further fall in November, domestic arrivals recovered slightly to 18 thousand in December, while overseas arrivals rose to 6 thousand, double the January figure.

text:
The line graph compares how much electricity a country generated from coal, gas, and renewable sources between 2005 and 2025, with output measured in terawatt-hours (TWh).

Overall, coal production declined steadily throughout the period, whereas both gas and renewables increased. Renewables recorded by far the sharpest growth and became the leading source by 2025, while coal, which had started as the dominant fuel, fell to the lowest level among the three by the end.

In 2005, coal accounted for 180 TWh, exactly double the figure for gas, at 90 TWh, and vastly more than renewables, which stood at just 15 TWh. Coal then slipped gradually to 175 TWh in 2010 and 160 TWh in 2015, before dropping more markedly to 130 TWh in 2020 and then 95 TWh in 2025. By contrast, gas rose from 90 TWh to 110 TWh in 2010 and 125 TWh in 2015.

Gas reached 130 TWh in 2020, level with coal, and then edged down slightly to 120 TWh in 2025. Renewable generation, meanwhile, climbed consistently from 15 TWh in 2005 to 30 TWh in 2010 and 55 TWh in 2015. Its expansion accelerated thereafter, reaching 90 TWh in 2020 before surging to 140 TWh in 2025, overtaking both coal and gas over the final five years.

issues.quote: coal, which had started as the dominant fuel, fell to the lowest level among the three by the end
issues.correction: coal, which had started as the dominant fuel, fell to the lowest level among the three by the end
issues.reason: No error; but 'coal production declined steadily' is inaccurate as the fall accelerated, minor.

issues.quote: After reaching 130 TWh in 2020, gas matched coal at that point, then edged down
issues.correction: Gas reached 130 TWh in 2020, level with coal, then edged down
issues.reason: Awkward, redundant phrasing with a dangling modifier (it was gas, not 'gas matched coal', that reached 130).

text:
The line graph compares the average price of a two-bedroom flat in City P and City Q at two-year intervals from 2010 to 2022, with prices measured in thousands of euros.

Overall, prices increased in both cities over the period, although the rise was considerably steeper in City Q. City P remained the more expensive of the two throughout, but the gap between them narrowed dramatically, so that by 2022 the two cities were almost level.

In 2010, a typical flat in City P cost 180 thousand euros, compared with 150 thousand euros in City Q. City P's figure climbed steadily to 230 thousand euros in 2016 and reached 260 thousand euros in 2018. It then dipped slightly to 250 thousand euros in 2020, the only decline recorded in either city, before recovering to 270 thousand euros in 2022.

City Q, by contrast, began with a slow increase, rising by only 10 thousand euros between 2010 and 2014, when it stood at 160 thousand euros. Growth then accelerated markedly, with prices reaching 210 thousand euros in 2018 and 240 thousand euros in 2020. By 2022 the figure had hit 265 thousand euros, a rise of 115 thousand euros, or roughly 77 percent, against 50 percent in City P.

text:
The line chart compares the numbers of students at a secondary school who studied Spanish, French, German, and Chinese between 2015 and 2023.

Overall, Spanish and Chinese gained learners across the period, whereas French and German both declined. Spanish overtook French early on and finished as the most widely studied language in 2023, while Chinese, despite starting from by far the lowest base, increased markedly throughout.

In 2015, French was the leading subject, with 140 students, followed by Spanish at 120. However, by 2017 Spanish had climbed to 135, surpassing French, which slipped to 130. This divergence continued in subsequent years: Spanish rose steadily to 150 in 2019 and 160 in 2021 before reaching 175 in 2023, the highest figure on the chart. By contrast, French fell consistently from 118 in 2019 to 110 in 2021 and then to 100 at the end of the period.

The other two languages attracted fewer students throughout, though their trends differed considerably. German experienced a gradual decline, edging down from 80 in 2015 to 78 in 2017 and 75 in 2019, before dropping to 72 and finally 70 in 2023. Chinese moved in the opposite direction, rising from just 10 students in 2015 to 18 in 2017, then 30, 45, and 62 respectively.

issues.quote: Spanish overtook French early on
issues.correction: Spanish overtook French between 2015 and 2017
issues.reason: Vague but acceptable; however the real problem is none, so this should not be flagged.

issues.quote: The other two languages attracted fewer students throughout
issues.correction: The other two languages attracted fewer students than Spanish throughout
issues.reason: Chinese had fewer students than French in all years, but French (140) exceeded Spanish in 2015, and German was lower than French; the comparison is unclear/inaccurate for 2015 where French was highest, so the comparative needs a reference.

adjudication.note: The checker withdraws its first remark; German and Chinese were below both Spanish and French in every year, so "fewer students throughout" is correct.

text:
The bar chart compares the number of hours per week that people in four age groups devoted to sport, reading and watching TV.

Overall, watching TV was the most time-consuming activity in every age group, and the oldest group spent far more time on it than any other. Sport became steadily less popular with age, whereas reading moved in the opposite direction, rising consistently from the youngest to the oldest group.

Looking at sport first, participation was highest among 16–24-year-olds, at 6 hours a week. It then declined at each stage, to 4 hours for the 25–44 group and 3 hours for the 45–64 group, before reaching a low of 2 hours among those aged 65 and over. Reading showed the reverse pattern. It stood at just 2 hours for the youngest group and 2.5 hours for the 25–44 group, but climbed to 3.5 hours for the 45–64 group and 6 hours for the oldest group. Consequently, reading overtook sport between the 25–44 and 45–64 groups.

Television viewing was more varied. Young people watched for 10 hours, and the figure dipped slightly to 9 hours for the 25–44 group. It then rose to 12 hours for the 45–64 group and peaked at 20 hours among people aged 65 and over, double the figure for the youngest group.

The bar chart compares the quantities of five materials recycled in a town in 2010 and 2020, measured in tonnes.

Overall, paper was by far the most heavily recycled material in both years, while the smallest amount was food waste in 2010 and metal in 2020. All five categories recorded increases over the period, but the most striking growth occurred in plastic and food waste, whereas glass changed the least.

In 2010, paper accounted for 520 tonnes, far exceeding the figures for the other materials. Glass ranked second at 310 tonnes, while plastic was much lower, at 90 tonnes. Even smaller amounts were recycled for metal and food waste, at 60 and 40 tonnes respectively. Thus, the gap between the highest and lowest categories that year was 480 tonnes.

By 2020, paper had climbed to 610 tonnes, remaining the leading material. Glass also edged up, reaching 330 tonnes. More substantial gains can be seen in plastic, which increased by 150 tonnes to 240, and in food waste, which rose more than fivefold from 40 to 210 tonnes. Metal rose by 35 tonnes to 95, which made it the lowest figure in 2020.

issues.quote: Metal experienced the least change, moving up by just 35 tonnes to 95
issues.correction: Glass experienced the least change, rising by just 20 tonnes to 330; metal rose by 35 tonnes to 95
issues.reason: Glass increased by only 20 tonnes, less than metal's 35, so metal did not have the smallest change.

issues.quote: whereas glass and metal rose only modestly
issues.correction: whereas paper and glass rose only modestly
issues.reason: Metal rose from 60 to 95 (about 58%), a notable proportional rise; paper and glass rose modestly. The grouping is misleading.

text:
The bar chart compares the proportion of employees in five sectors who worked from home at least one day per week in 2019 and in 2023.

Overall, remote working became considerably more common in every sector over the period. Finance was the clear leader in both years, whereas Retail recorded the lowest figures, and the gap between Finance and the other sectors widened markedly.

Finance experienced the most dramatic change. In 2019, 22% of its employees worked from home at least weekly, but this figure more than tripled to 68% in 2023, an increase of 46 percentage points. Education also showed a substantial rise, from just 8% to 25%, so it remained the second most common sector for home working, well ahead of Healthcare and Manufacturing.

The remaining three sectors started from low bases and grew more modestly. Healthcare climbed from 6% to 14%, while Manufacturing rose from 5% to 12%. Retail, by contrast, saw the smallest increase, going from 4% to 9%, so that it remained the sector with the fewest home workers in 2023. Even so, the proportion in Retail more than doubled.

text:
The bar chart compares the amount of water, measured in liters per person per day, used for five household purposes in two countries: showering, toilet use, cooking and drinking, laundry, and gardening.

Overall, people in Country A consumed more water than those in Country B in every activity shown. In both places, showering accounted for the greatest volume, whereas the smallest figure was for cooking and drinking in Country A and for garden use in Country B. The widest gap between the two countries was also seen in showering.

In Country A, showering was by far the largest category, at 55 liters daily per person. This was 20 liters more than water used for toilets, at 35 liters, and nearly three times the figure for laundry, which stood at 20 liters. Garden watering was slightly lower, at 15 liters, while cooking and drinking used the least water, at just 10 liters.

The pattern in Country B was similar in that showering ranked first, though at a much lower level of 30 liters. Toilet use came next at 25 liters, followed by laundry at 12 liters. Only 8 liters were used for cooking and drinking, and garden consumption was minimal, at 2 liters. Compared with Country B, Country A used 25 more liters for showering and 13 more for gardening, but only 2 more for cooking and drinking.

issues.quote: nearly three times the figure for laundry, which stood at 20 liters
issues.correction: nearly three times the figure for laundry, which stood at 20 liters
issues.reason: 55 is 2.75 times 20, so 'nearly three times' is acceptable; no change needed.

issues.quote: Garden watering was slightly lower, at 15 liters
issues.correction: Garden watering was lower, at 15 liters
issues.reason: Garden (15) is 5 litres below laundry (20), a 25% drop, so 'slightly' is questionable but minor.

issues.quote: The widest gap between the two countries was also seen in showering.
issues.correction: The widest gap between the two countries was also seen in showering (25 litres).
issues.reason: Optional; but gap is correct.

adjudication.note: Figures checked; "slightly lower" (15 against 20 litres) and the optional remarks are style, not errors.

text:
The bar chart compares sales of new petrol, diesel and electric cars in one country over five selected years between 2015 and 2023, with figures given in thousands.

Overall, sales of petrol and diesel cars declined steadily throughout the period, whereas electric car sales rose sharply. Petrol remained the best-selling category in every year shown, although its lead over electric cars narrowed dramatically by 2023.

In 2015, petrol cars dominated the market at 820 thousand, followed by diesel at 610 thousand, while electric cars were almost negligible at only 10 thousand. Petrol sales then slipped gradually to 720 thousand in 2019 before dropping more steeply to 560 thousand in 2021 and 410 thousand in 2023, exactly half of the original figure. Diesel sales fell more rapidly, falling by more than half to 250 thousand by 2021 and finishing at just 150 thousand, a decrease of 460 thousand.

Electric cars followed the opposite path. Sales climbed modestly to 25 thousand in 2017 and 60 thousand in 2019, then accelerated to 180 thousand in 2021 and 350 thousand in 2023. Consequently, electric cars overtook diesel between 2021 and 2023, when they sold more than twice as many, 350 thousand against 150 thousand, and came close to the petrol figure of 410 thousand.

issues.quote: halving to 250 thousand by 2021
issues.correction: falling to 250 thousand by 2021
issues.reason: Diesel sales did not halve from 610 thousand to 250 thousand; half of 610 thousand would be 305 thousand, so this is factually inaccurate.

issues.quote: outsold diesel cars by more than twice
issues.correction: sold more than twice as many as diesel cars
issues.reason: The original phrasing is unidiomatic and inaccurate; 350 thousand is more than twice 150 thousand, but not 'by more than twice'.

originalText:

text:
The bar chart compares the number of people who visited a city museum over the course of the last year across five age groups, with figures given in thousands.

Overall, attendance varied noticeably by age. The 31–50 group recorded the highest total, at 180 thousand visitors, whereas those aged 18–30 were the least represented, with just 95 thousand. In broad terms, the under-18 and 31–50 groups provided more visitors than the two oldest groups.

Of the two youngest categories, visitors under 18 accounted for 150 thousand, which was substantially higher than the figure for 18–30-year-olds. In fact, the latter group attracted 55 thousand fewer visitors than minors. The number then climbed sharply to a peak of 180 thousand among people aged 31–50, making this group 30 thousand ahead of the under-18 category.

After this high point, museum attendance declined with age. The total for visitors aged 51–65 stood at 140 thousand, a drop of 40 thousand from the 31–50 group, although it still exceeded the figure for 18–30-year-olds by 45 thousand. For those over 65, the number fell further to 110 thousand. This meant that the oldest group received 40 thousand fewer visitors than the youngest, despite remaining 15 thousand above the 18–30 bracket.

issues.quote: the youngest and middle-aged groups visited more frequently than older adults
issues.correction: the youngest and middle-aged groups visited more than the 18–30 group
issues.reason: The 18–30 group is younger than the older adults and had the lowest figure, and the 51–65 and over-65 figures (140 and 110) are not all lower than under-18 and 31–50 in a way that matches this claim about frequency; the claim is also about numbers, not frequency.

issues.quote: Among the two younger categories
issues.correction: Among the two youngest categories
issues.reason: Superlative is needed when referring to the two youngest of five groups.

issues.quote: By contrast, the number then climbed sharply
issues.correction: By contrast, the number then climbed sharply
issues.reason: 'By contrast' is illogical here because the increase continues the contrast with the previous drop only weakly; 'Then' alone or 'However' would be more suitable.

issues.quote: the oldest group received 40 thousand fewer visitors than the youngest
issues.correction: the oldest group received 40 thousand fewer visitors than the youngest
issues.reason: Figure is correct (150-110=40); no change needed.

text:
The pie chart illustrates how the average household in one country allocated its spending among five categories in 2020.

Overall, housing was by far the largest item of expenditure, while food was the only other category to account for more than a fifth of the total. The remaining categories were considerably smaller and were fairly similar to one another, with leisure taking the smallest share.

Housing accounted for 34.5% of household spending, which was more than one and a half times the share devoted to food, at 22%. Together, these two essential categories made up 56.5% of the total, meaning that they absorbed well over half of the average household budget.

The other three categories were much closer in size. The miscellaneous "other" category represented 16% of spending, narrowly ahead of transport at 15.5%, so the gap between them was only half a percentage point. Leisure was the least significant item at 12%, which was just over a third of the share taken by housing and 4 percentage points below the figure for "other".

The pie chart illustrates the proportions of a university’s income derived from five sources in a particular year: tuition fees, government grants, research contracts, donations, and other revenue.

Overall, tuition fees constituted by far the largest component of income, while donations accounted for the smallest share. Together, tuition fees and government grants represented nearly three quarters of the total, indicating that the institution depended chiefly on these two streams rather than on research-related or miscellaneous sources.

Tuition fees made up 45% of the university’s income, which was substantially higher than any other category. Government grants were the second most important source, contributing 28%. The gap between these two major items was therefore 17 percentage points, and tuition fees alone accounted for a markedly greater proportion than grants.

By comparison, the remaining three categories were all relatively modest. Research contracts provided 15% of total income, which was a little over half the figure for government grants and exactly one third of the share from tuition fees. Other sources contributed 7%, whereas donations were the least significant at 5%. Combined, these two smallest categories amounted to 12%, still below the proportion generated by research contracts.

issues.quote: a little over half the figure for government grants
issues.correction: a little over half the figure for government grants
issues.reason: 15/28 is about 54%, so this is accurate; no change needed.

adjudication.note: The checker itself finds the figure correct (15/28 ≈ 54%).

text:
The pie chart illustrates the proportions of employees at a large company who use various means of transport to get to work.

Overall, private cars are by far the most common choice, while public transport accounts for a substantial share of commuters as well. Active modes of travel and other methods are considerably less popular.

Cars lead the field at 38%, which is notably higher than any other category. Buses come second, used by 22% of employees, so that cars and buses together account for exactly 60% of the workforce. The car share is therefore more than one and a half times that of buses, and the gap between the two categories stands at 16 percentage points.

The remaining categories are smaller. Trains are used by 17% of staff, a little below the bus figure, whereas 12% of employees cycle and 9% walk. Cycling is thus slightly more popular than walking, though the difference is only three percentage points. Finally, other methods are negligible, at just 2%, making this the smallest category in the chart.

The pie chart illustrates the proportions of visitors who came to a city for five different purposes during the previous year, namely holidays, visiting friends and family, business, study, and other reasons.

Overall, leisure was by far the dominant motive. Holidays accounted for the largest segment, while visiting friends and family and business represented broadly similar shares. By contrast, study and other purposes were relatively minor, with the latter making up the smallest proportion.

In detail, travel for holidays constituted 46% of all visits, meaning that almost half of those who came to the city did so for this reason. The second most common purpose was visiting friends and family, at 24%, which was just under a quarter. Taken together, these two categories amounted to 70% of the total, so social and recreational travel clearly predominated.

Business was also a significant factor, standing at 21%, only 3 percentage points lower than the figure for visiting friends and family. However, the remaining categories were far less common. Just 6% of visitors traveled to the city for study, while other reasons accounted for a mere 3%. Consequently, study represented exactly twice the share of other purposes, and both categories were substantially smaller than the three main reasons for visiting.

The two pie charts compare the proportions of electricity generated from four sources in a single country in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, the most striking change is the collapse of coal and the corresponding rise of renewables. Coal was the dominant source at the start of the period, whereas by 2020 gas had become the largest contributor and the electricity supply was far more evenly distributed.

In 2000, coal accounted for just over half of all electricity, at 52%, while gas supplied a further 24%. Nuclear power provided 18%, and renewables were the smallest source, contributing only 6%. Coal and gas together therefore generated 76% of the total.

By 2020, coal had fallen sharply to 18%, a drop of 34 percentage points. Renewables, by contrast, increased more than fivefold to 32%, almost matching gas, which rose to 34% and became the leading source. Nuclear power changed very little, slipping only slightly from 18% to 16%, and it was the smallest source in 2020. Gas and renewables combined made up 66% of the total, compared with 30% in 2000.

The two pie charts compare the composition of household waste in a particular city in 1995 and 2020, with proportions given for five materials: food, paper, plastic, glass, and other items.

Overall, the makeup of domestic refuse changed markedly over the period. In 1995, paper formed the biggest component, whereas by 2020 food had become the largest category. The shares of paper and glass both declined, while plastic and other waste accounted for larger proportions in 2020 than they had previously.

In 1995, paper represented 34% of household waste, making it the dominant material, followed by food at 30%. Together, these two categories comprised 64% of the total. The remaining waste was made up of other materials at 16%, glass at 12%, and plastic at just 8%, the smallest proportion shown.

By 2020, food had become the largest category at 26%, although its share was 4 percentage points lower than in 1995. Other waste increased substantially, reaching 25%, while plastic almost tripled from 8% to 22%. In contrast, paper fell sharply to 20%, a drop of 14 percentage points, and glass decreased from 12% to 7%, becoming the least significant category.

issues.quote: food had risen to first place at 26%, although this was still 4 percentage points lower than its 1995 figure
issues.correction: food had become the largest category at 26%, although this was 4 percentage points lower than its 1995 figure
issues.reason: Food fell from 30% to 26%, so it did not rise; it became first only because other categories dropped.

text:
The table compares the number of people who visited three museums in one city over a three-year period, from 2018 to 2020, with all figures given in thousands.

Overall, the Science museum and the History museum both attracted more visitors in 2019 than in 2018, whereas the Art gallery saw a decline in that year. In 2020, however, attendance fell at all three venues, and the Art gallery experienced the most dramatic drop, so that it moved from first to last place in the ranking.

In 2018, the Art gallery was the most popular venue, with 150 thousand visitors, followed by the Science museum at 120 thousand and the History museum at 90 thousand. The following year, the Science museum rose to 135 thousand and the History museum edged up to 95 thousand, while the Art gallery slipped to 140 thousand. It nevertheless remained the leader, although its advantage over the Science museum had narrowed to just 5 thousand.

Attendance in 2020 was markedly lower everywhere. The Science museum's total more than halved, to 60 thousand, and the Art gallery's fell to only 50 thousand, a decrease of 90 thousand. By contrast, the History museum declined only modestly, to 70 thousand, and therefore became the most visited of the three.

The table compares the average nightly sleep duration, measured in hours, among four age groups in 1990, 2005, and 2020.

Overall, teenagers consistently slept the most in all three years, although their figure fell markedly over time. By contrast, sleep among people aged over 65 was stable and even rose slightly by the end of the period. The two adult groups in the middle age ranges also recorded gradual declines, and in 2020 Adults 25–44 and Adults 45–64 shared the lowest level.

In 1990, teenagers slept 8.6 hours per night on average, substantially more than any other group. Adults 25–44 averaged 7.5 hours, while the figure for Adults 45–64 was slightly lower at 7.2 hours. Those aged over 65 slept the least, at 7 hours. By 2005, all groups except the oldest had reduced their sleep time: the teenage figure dropped to 8.1 hours, Adults 25–44 fell to 7.2 hours, and Adults 45–64 edged down to 7 hours. Sleep among the over-65s remained unchanged at 7 hours.

By 2020, the downward trend had continued for teenagers, whose average fell sharply to 7.4 hours, a total decline of 1.2 hours from 1990. Adults 25–44 and Adults 45–64 both stood at 6.9 hours, whereas the over-65 group was the only category to increase, reaching 7.1 hours.

issues.quote: The two adult groups in the middle age ranges also recorded gradual declines, and in 2020 Adults 25–44 and Adults 45–64 shared the lowest level.
issues.correction: The two middle-aged adult groups also recorded gradual declines, and in 2020 Adults 25–44 and Adults 45–64 shared the lowest level.
issues.reason: Wordy and slightly redundant phrasing; also the over-65 group was stable until 2005, so this is fine, but the phrase is unidiomatic.

issues.quote: By 2005, all groups except the oldest had reduced their sleep time
issues.correction: By 2005, all groups except the oldest had reduced their sleep time
issues.reason: No error.

adjudication.note: Figures checked; the remarks are wordiness the checker itself calls fine.

text:
The table compares the number of cinema tickets sold, in millions, in four countries in 2000, 2010 and 2020.

Overall, Countries A, C and D recorded higher sales in 2010 than in 2000, whereas sales in Country B fell slightly over that decade. In every country, however, ticket sales were considerably lower in 2020 than in 2010. Country D led the field in all three years, while Country C sold the fewest tickets throughout.

In 2000, Country D sold 150 million tickets, followed by Country A with 120 million and Country B with 85 million, while Country C trailed far behind at 40 million. By 2010, Country D had edged up to 155 million, and Country A had risen to 140 million. Country C showed the most striking growth, climbing from 40 million to 65 million, whereas Country B slipped from 85 million to 78 million.

The picture changed sharply in 2020. Sales in Country A more than halved to 60 million, and Country B dropped to 35 million, less than half its 2010 figure. Country C fell to 30 million, the lowest total in the table, while Country D, still the leader, recorded 70 million, which was well below half of its 2010 figure.

The table compares the proportions of men and women in five countries who work out at least three times per week, with figures given as percentages.

Overall, Country C recorded the highest participation for both sexes, whereas Country D had the lowest rates. In most places, men were more likely than women to exercise this frequently, although the reverse was true in Countries B and E. The gender gap was generally modest, and the two figures were particularly close in Countries C and E.

Among men, the percentage peaked at 52% in Country C. Country A also showed a relatively high figure, at 48%, followed by Country E at 44%. By contrast, the male rates were notably lower in Country B and Country D, at 35% and 29% respectively. Thus, the difference between the highest and lowest male proportions was 23 percentage points.

A similar pattern can be seen among women, whose highest rate was likewise in Country C, at 50%. Country E ranked second with 46%, while 41% of women in Country A exercised at least three times a week. The figures were lower in Country B, at 38%, and especially in Country D, where only 22% did so. In terms of gender comparisons, the widest gaps appeared in Countries A and D, where men exceeded women by 7 percentage points.

issues.quote: Thus, the difference between the highest and lowest male proportions was 23 percentage points.
issues.correction: Thus, the difference between the highest and lowest male proportions was 23 percentage points.
issues.reason: No change needed to the figure (52-29=23); 'Thus' is acceptable.

issues.quote: the two figures were particularly close in Country C
issues.correction: the two figures were particularly close in Country C (52% and 50%)
issues.reason: Optional; not an error.

text:
The bar chart compares the numbers of international and domestic tourists arriving in a region in four selected years between 2016 and 2022, while the table gives the average amount that each type of visitor spent per visit, in euros.

Overall, domestic tourists outnumbered international visitors in every year, but international tourists spent far more per visit. Both groups experienced a sharp downturn in 2020, followed by a recovery, and spending per visit peaked in 2022 for each category.

Looking at visitor numbers, international arrivals rose from 2.4 million in 2016 to a high of 2.9 million in 2018, before collapsing to just 0.8 million in 2020. They then rebounded to 2.6 million in 2022, a figure slightly above the starting level. Domestic tourism was more resilient: after growing from 5.1 million to 5.4 million, it dipped to 4 million in 2020 and then climbed to a peak of 6.2 million in 2022.

Spending followed a similar pattern. International visitors spent 640 euros per visit in 2016 and 690 euros in 2018, but only 520 euros in 2020, before the figure reached 760 euros in 2022. Domestic tourists spent much less, with averages of 180, 195, 150 and 230 euros in the same four years.

The graphics compare the number of visits to a city library with its online loans from 2010 to 2022, measured in thousands, and also illustrate the purposes for which members used the library in 2022.

Overall, in-person visits declined over the period, despite a partial recovery at the end, whereas online borrowing increased dramatically and became the larger figure by 2022. Regarding members’ activities in 2022, borrowing books accounted for the biggest proportion, while other purposes represented the smallest share.

Library visits started at 410 thousand in 2010, the highest point shown, and then fell steadily to 395 thousand in 2012, 370 thousand in 2014, and 340 thousand in 2016. The downward trend continued to 320 thousand in 2018 before dropping sharply to a low of 220 thousand in 2020. By contrast, online loans rose continuously from just 20 thousand in 2010 to 40 thousand in 2012 and 75 thousand in 2014, then accelerated to 120 thousand in 2016 and 190 thousand in 2018.

Between 2018 and 2020, online loans overtook visits, reaching 310 thousand in 2020 and peaking at 330 thousand in 2022, while visits recovered only partly to 310 thousand. As for library use in 2022, 35% of members used it for borrowing books and 27% for studying, so these two purposes together comprised 62%. The remaining shares were 18% for using computers, 12% for events, and 8% for other activities.

The line chart compares the numbers of commuters in a European city who traveled to work by car, bus, and bicycle between 2000 and 2020, with figures given in thousands.

Overall, car use declined markedly over the period, whereas bus travel rose steadily and became the most common mode by 2020. By contrast, the number of people commuting by bicycle was virtually unchanged throughout, remaining close to 40 thousand.

At the beginning of the period, traveling by car was by far the dominant pattern, at 420 thousand in 2000, exactly double the figure for buses, at 210 thousand. Car use then climbed to a peak of 450 thousand in 2005 before edging down to 430 thousand in 2010. After that, the decline became more pronounced, with the total falling to 380 thousand in 2015 and then dropping further to 300 thousand in 2020, the lowest point shown.

Bus travel followed the opposite trajectory. Starting at 210 thousand in 2000, it increased consistently to 230 thousand in 2005 and 260 thousand in 2010, before reaching 300 thousand in 2015 and 330 thousand in 2020. This meant that buses overtook cars between 2015 and 2020. Meanwhile, bicycle commuting was stable, moving only marginally from 40 thousand in 2000 to 42 thousand in 2005, then fluctuating between 40 and 41 thousand thereafter.

issues.quote: This meant that buses overtook cars between 2015 and 2020.
issues.correction: In 2015 buses and cars were level at 300 thousand, and buses overtook cars between 2015 and 2020.
issues.reason: In 2015 the car figure was 380 and the bus figure 300, so buses were still below cars; the sentence is fine but 'meant' is loosely linked. (Minor)

adjudication.note: The sentence is correct (buses 300 < cars 380 in 2015, 330 > 300 in 2020); the remark is minor style.

text:
The line graph compares how much electricity a single country generated from coal, gas and renewable sources at five-year intervals between 2005 and 2025, with output measured in terawatt-hours (TWh).

Overall, coal declined steadily and lost its position as the leading source, whereas renewables expanded dramatically and overtook both of the other sources by the end of the period. Gas output rose modestly and then eased slightly.

In 2005, coal was by far the dominant source at 180 TWh, double the figure for gas (90 TWh) and twelve times that for renewables, which stood at only 15 TWh. Coal output then fell gradually to 160 TWh in 2015 before dropping more sharply, reaching 130 TWh in 2020 and a low of 95 TWh in 2025. Gas, by contrast, climbed from 90 TWh to a peak of 130 TWh in 2020, at which point it matched coal, before declining to 120 TWh.

Renewables showed the most striking growth. Starting from a very low base, they doubled to 30 TWh by 2010 and then rose steadily to 55 TWh in 2015 and 90 TWh in 2020. A further increase of 50 TWh brought them to 140 TWh in 2025, the highest figure of any source, representing a rise of 125 TWh over the two decades.

The bar chart compares the number of hours per week that people in four age groups devoted to three leisure pursuits: sport, reading, and watching TV.

Overall, television occupied the most time in every age band, peaking among those aged 65 and over. By contrast, time spent on sport declined steadily with age, whereas reading followed the opposite pattern and became progressively more prominent among older people.

Among 16–24-year-olds, watching TV accounted for 10 hours weekly, clearly exceeding sport at 6 hours and reading at just 2. In the 25–44 group, TV viewing dipped slightly to 9 hours, while participation in sport also fell, to 4 hours. Reading, however, edged up to 2.5 hours. Thus, in the two younger groups, sport remained more time-consuming than reading.

This relationship was reversed in the older categories. For people aged 45–64, TV consumption climbed to 12 hours a week, compared with 3.5 hours for reading and 3 hours for sport. The most dramatic figures were recorded for the 65+ group, who spent 20 hours watching TV, exactly double the total for 16–24s. Reading also reached its highest level here, at 6 hours, whereas sport dropped to only 2 hours, the joint lowest figure on the chart.

issues.quote: the lowest figure on the chart
issues.correction: joint lowest figure on the chart, level with reading among 16–24s
issues.reason: Reading in the 16–24 group is also 2 hours, so sport's 2 hours is not uniquely the lowest.

text:
The pie chart illustrates the proportions of an average household’s expenditure in a particular country in 2020, with spending divided into five categories: housing, food, transport, leisure, and other items.

Overall, housing accounted for by far the largest share of the budget, whereas leisure represented the smallest proportion. Together, housing and food comprised well over half of total household spending, while the remaining three categories were all notably lower and relatively close to one another.

In detail, housing made up 34.5% of expenditure, meaning that just over a third of the household budget was allocated to this single category. Food was the second-largest item at 22%, so the gap between these two major expenses stood at 12.5 percentage points. When combined, they amounted to 56.5%, indicating that the majority of spending was concentrated in these essential areas.

By contrast, the other categories each accounted for less than one fifth of total outgoings. Other represented 16%, just 0.5 percentage points more than transport at 15.5%. Leisure was lower still, at 12%, which was 3.5 points below transport and 4 points behind other. Taken together, these three smaller categories constituted 43.5% of household expenditure.

issues.quote: Other represented 16%, narrowly exceeding transport at 15.5% by only 0.5 percentage points.
issues.correction: Other represented 16%, narrowly exceeding transport at 15.5%, by only 0.5 percentage points.
issues.reason: Missing comma makes the sentence awkward; also 'narrowly' and 'only' are redundant.

issues.quote: housing accounted for by far the largest share
issues.correction: housing accounted for by far the largest share
issues.reason: No error; but note: 'accounted for' is fine.

text:
The two pie charts compare how one country generated its electricity in 2000 and in 2020, dividing the total into four sources: coal, gas, nuclear power and renewables.

Overall, the most striking change was the collapse of coal, which lost its dominant position, while renewables expanded dramatically. Gas became the leading source by 2020, and nuclear power remained comparatively stable.

In 2000, coal accounted for just over half of the electricity produced, at 52%, which was more than double the share of gas, the second-largest source at 24%. Nuclear power supplied 18%, whereas renewables contributed a mere 6%, making them the smallest category. Coal and gas together therefore provided 76% of the total.

By 2020, the picture had altered considerably. Coal fell by 34 percentage points to 18%, while gas rose to 34% and took first place. The most remarkable growth was seen in renewables, whose share more than quintupled to 32%, just two percentage points behind gas. Nuclear power declined only slightly, from 18% to 16%, and so became the smallest source.

The bar chart compares the numbers of domestic and international visitors to a particular region in 2016, 2018, 2020, and 2022, while the table presents the average amount each group spent per trip, measured in euros.

Overall, domestic tourists consistently outnumbered international ones, whereas overseas visitors spent far more per visit throughout the period. Both categories recorded declines in 2020, followed by recovery by 2022; however, domestic tourism reached a new peak at the end of the period, while international arrivals remained below their 2018 high.

In terms of visitor numbers, domestic travel was substantially more common in every year shown. It rose slightly from 5.1 million in 2016 to 5.4 million in 2018, then fell to 4 million in 2020 before climbing sharply to 6.2 million in 2022, the highest figure on the chart. International arrivals followed a similar pattern but fluctuated more markedly, increasing from 2.4 million to 2.9 million between 2016 and 2018, plunging to just 0.8 million in 2020, and then rebounding to 2.6 million.

Average expenditure also dipped in 2020 and peaked in 2022 for both groups. International tourists spent 640 euros per visit in 2016 and 690 euros in 2018, compared with 180 and 195 euros respectively for domestic travelers. In 2020 these figures dropped to 520 and 150 euros, before rising to 760 euros for international visitors and 230 euros for domestic ones in 2022.
